questions.q: Which part of SQL is closest to fully standardized across platforms, with the least dialect divergence?
options: Basic SELECT / FROM / WHERE / ORDER BY queries
Procedural extensions like stored procedures and control flow
Auto-incrementing primary key syntax
Pagination syntax for returning the top N rows
questions.explain: Basic querying is where the ANSI/ISO standard is strongest and every platform in this course agrees almost completely.

options: Microsoft SQL Server's own dialect of SQL, built on the ANSI/ISO standard plus its own extensions
A separate database product unrelated to SQL Server
The official name for the ANSI/ISO SQL standard itself
Oracle's procedural SQL extension
questions.explain: T-SQL is SQL Server's dialect, not a different language — it implements the standard core and adds Microsoft-specific extensions.

questions.q: Which of the three reasons for dialect divergence explains why procedural code (stored procedures, control flow) looks so different between T-SQL and PL/SQL?
options: The ANSI/ISO standard never fully standardized procedural extensions, leaving vendors to build their own
Procedural code is actually identical across platforms
Oracle refuses to follow any ANSI standards at all
Microsoft invented procedural SQL and other vendors copied it exactly
questions.explain: The standard is deliberately incomplete on procedural extensions, which is exactly why T-SQL and PL/SQL diverge so much in that area.

questions.q: According to this course's scope, what will you NOT find taught here?
options: Database administration topics like backup/restore, user security, and performance tuning internals
How data types differ between SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
How procedural code (stored procedures, error handling) differs across platforms
How basic query syntax like pagination differs across platforms
questions.explain: This course is scoped to the SQL language itself; administration is covered by LTV Academy's separate DBA-focused courses.

questions.q: Why do Oracle's CONNECT BY and SQL Server's CROSS APPLY both exist as proprietary extensions?
options: Vendors added them for competitive differentiation, solving real problems before the standard addressed them
They are required by the ANSI/ISO SQL standard
They are identical syntax that just has two different names
They were added by a third-party open-source project, not the vendors themselves
questions.explain: Competitive differentiation is one of the three reasons dialects diverge — vendors build proprietary solutions ahead of the standard.
